title: Fallacy Catalog
description: A plain, sourced catalog of named logical fallacies. Each entry gives a standard name, common aliases, a category, a short definition in plain words, an original example, a note on when the same pattern is not a fallacy (where the references give one), and the published references that list it.

entries.name: Accent
entries.definition: Changing the meaning of a statement by stressing a particular word or by lifting emphasis from its context, then reasoning from the shifted meaning.
entries.example: 'We should not speak ILL of our friends', so it's fine to speak ill of strangers.

entries.name: Accident
aliases: a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid
entries.definition: Applying a general rule to a case that is an exception, ignoring the circumstances that make the rule not apply.
entries.example: Cutting people with knives is a crime. Surgeons cut people with knives. So surgeons are criminals.

entries.name: Ad hoc rescue
entries.definition: Saving a cherished claim from contrary evidence by inventing an explanation that has no support except that it saves the claim.
entries.example: The psychic failed because the sceptics' negative energy blocked her powers.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: A new auxiliary hypothesis is fine if it is independently testable and later supported.

entries.name: Ad hominem (abusive)
entries.definition: Rejecting a claim or argument by attacking the person who made it rather than the reasons they gave.
entries.example: Why listen to his tax plan? He's been divorced three times.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: A person's record can be relevant when the question is whether to trust their testimony (for example, a witness with a history of lying) rather than whether their argument is sound. Arguing from an opponent's own stated commitments (Locke's sense of ad hominem) is also not a fallacy.

entries.definition: A syllogism with at least one negative premise but an affirmative conclusion.

entries.name: Affirming a disjunct
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'P or Q' and 'P' to 'not Q', as if 'or' always meant 'one but not both'.
entries.example: She's either talented or hardworking. She's talented, so she isn't hardworking.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Valid when the two options really do exclude each other.

entries.name: Affirming the consequent
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'If P then Q' and 'Q' to 'P'. Q could be true for some other reason.
entries.example: If the pipes burst, the floor is wet. The floor is wet. So the pipes burst.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: As a guess about the best explanation it can be reasonable evidence, provided the other possible causes are checked; it just isn't proof.

entries.name: Ambiguous middle term
entries.definition: A syllogism whose shared middle term is used in two different senses, so the premises do not really connect; a case of equivocation and of four terms.
entries.example: All banks are beside rivers. My savings are in a bank. So my savings are beside a river.

entries.name: Amphiboly
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from a sentence whose grammar allows two readings, relying on the reading that wasn't meant.
entries.example: The sign says 'Fine for parking here', so parking here must be fine.

entries.name: Anecdotal evidence
entries.definition: Relying on a personal story or a few vivid cases instead of more representative evidence.
entries.example: My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that harmful.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Anecdotes can suggest hypotheses or illustrate well-supported findings.

entries.definition: Projecting human qualities such as intentions or feelings onto something that isn't human and reasoning from that projection.

entries.name: Appeal to authority (illegitimate)
entries.definition: Accepting a claim because someone said it when that person is not a genuine expert on the question, the experts disagree, or the authority is being treated as settling the matter regardless of the evidence.
entries.example: A famous physicist says this diet cures cancer, so it does.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Relying on a genuine expert speaking within their field, where experts broadly agree, is reasonable and not a fallacy.

entries.name: Argument from fallacy
entries.definition: Inferring that a claim is false because someone defended it badly. True claims can have bad arguments offered for them.
entries.example: Your argument for vaccination was a slippery slope, so vaccines must not work.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Fine to conclude that the argument fails to support the claim; the error is concluding the claim is false.

entries.name: Argument from ignorance
entries.definition: Treating a lack of disproof as proof, or a lack of proof as disproof.
entries.example: No one has proved that ghosts don't exist, so they do.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: A careful search that would probably have found something can count as evidence that it isn't there.

entries.definition: Concluding that something is false (or must have an extraordinary cause) because you find it hard to believe or imagine.

entries.definition: Repeating an argument until others stop responding, then treating their silence as agreement.

entries.name: Baconian fallacy
entries.definition: Supposing that historians can reach the whole truth simply by piling up individual pieces of evidence, without questions or theories to guide them.
entries.example: Collect every document from the period and the meaning of the war will become obvious.

entries.name: Bad seed
entries.definition: Undermining someone's reasoning by pointing to their family history or background when that history is irrelevant.
entries.example: His father was a con man, so don't trust his business proposal.

entries.name: Bandwagon
entries.definition: Arguing that a claim is correct because more and more people are coming to believe it.
entries.example: Everyone's switching to this phone, so it must be the best.

entries.name: Base-rate fallacy
entries.definition: Judging a probability from specific evidence (such as a test result) while ignoring how common the thing is to begin with.
entries.example: The test is 99% accurate and I tested positive, so I almost certainly have this disease that affects 1 in 100,000 people.

entries.name: Begging the question
entries.definition: Supporting a conclusion with premises that already assume it, so the argument gives no independent reason.
entries.example: Her advice is trustworthy because she's an honest person, and she's honest because her advice is trustworthy.

entries.name: Composition
entries.definition: Assuming that what is true of the parts, or of each member, must be true of the whole or the group.

entries.example: Oxygen is needed for fire. There is oxygen in this room, so there will be a fire.

sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Modal fallacy"

entries.name: Conjunction fallacy
entries.definition: Judging that two things together are more likely than one of them alone. A combination can never be more probable than either part.
entries.example: Sam is likelier to be a librarian who reads poetry than to be a librarian.

entries.name: Converse accident
entries.definition: Generalizing from exceptional cases to a rule meant for ordinary cases.
entries.example: Patients in pain are allowed morphine, so everyone should be allowed morphine.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Converse Accident"

entries.name: Courtier's reply
entries.definition: Dismissing a criticism by claiming the critic hasn't studied the subject in enough depth to comment, without answering the criticism.
entries.example: You can't criticise astrology until you've read the major astrological texts.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Expertise can matter when the criticism actually depends on a misunderstanding the critic could fix by learning more.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Courtier's reply"

entries.name: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: with this, therefore because of this
entries.definition: Concluding that because two things occur together, one causes the other.
entries.example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, so ice cream causes drowning.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Correlation is a reason to look for a causal link, not proof of one.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Cum Hoc, Ergo Propter Hoc"

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Cum hoc ergo propter hoc"

entries.name: Curve fitting
entries.definition: Building a model or explanation so closely around existing data, noise included, that it fits the past well but predicts poorly.
entries.example: Our 30-variable formula explains every past election perfectly, so it will predict the next one.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Curve Fitting"

entries.name: Dangling comparative
entries.definition: Using a comparative word like 'better' or 'more' without saying what is being compared to, so the claim sounds meaningful but can't be checked.
entries.example: Our toothpaste cleans 50% better!

entries.name: Definist fallacy
entries.definition: Defining a term unfairly so that a controversial position becomes easier to defend, or treating one property as identical with another without argument.
entries.example: By 'education' I mean job training, so an art history degree isn't education.

entries.name: Definitional retreat
entries.definition: Changing the meaning of a key word once an objection is raised, so the claim survives in name only.
entries.example: When I said the plan 'worked', I meant it started a conversation.

entries.name: Denying a conjunct
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'not both P and Q' and 'not P' to 'Q'. Both could be false.
entries.example: You can't be both at the office and at the gym. You're not at the office, so you must be at the gym.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Valid only if exactly one of the two must be true.

entries.name: Denying the antecedent
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'If P then Q' and 'not P' to 'not Q'. Q could still be true for some other reason.
entries.example: If it rains, the game is cancelled. It didn't rain. So the game wasn't cancelled.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Valid when the conditional really means 'if and only if'.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Denying the Antecedent"

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Propositional fallacies", item "Denying the antecedent"

entries.name: Disregarding known science
entries.definition: Making a claim that ignores or contradicts well-established science without addressing it.
entries.example: This engine runs forever on a single tank of water.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Established science can be challenged, but the challenge must engage the evidence for it.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Disregarding Known Science"

entries.name: Division
entries.definition: Assuming that what is true of a whole or group must be true of each of its parts or members.
entries.example: The university is world-famous, so every professor there is world-famous.

entries.name: Division of words (Aristotle)
entries.definition: Aristotle's fallacy of splitting apart words that should be read together, which changes the meaning, as in '5 is 2 and 3, so 5 is even and odd'.
entries.example: Five is two and three; two is even and three is odd; so five is both even and odd.

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: Doorman fallacy
entries.definition: Reducing a role to its most visible task and judging its value or cost on that basis, missing the less visible value it provides.
entries.example: A doorman just opens doors, so replace him with an automatic door.

entries.name: Double counting
entries.definition: Counting the same outcome or piece of evidence more than once, so probabilities or totals come out too high.
entries.example: There's a 50% chance of rain Saturday and 50% Sunday, so it's certain to rain this weekend.

entries.name: Double standard
entries.definition: Judging two relevantly similar people or cases by different standards.
entries.example: When our candidate changes his mind it's growth; when theirs does it's flip-flopping.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Double Standard"

entries.name: Ecological fallacy
entries.definition: Drawing conclusions about individuals from statistics about the groups they belong to.
entries.example: Richer states vote for party X, so richer people vote for party X.

entries.name: I'm entitled to my opinion
entries.definition: Treating the right to hold an opinion as if it were a reason the opinion is correct or exempt from criticism.
entries.example: You can show me all the data you want; I'm entitled to my opinion.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "I'm entitled to my opinion"

entries.name: Equivocation
entries.definition: Using a word or phrase in one sense in one part of an argument and in a different sense in another, so the argument only seems to work.
entries.example: A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark.

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: Etymological fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that a word's original or historical meaning is its real or current meaning.
entries.example: 'Decimate' originally meant killing one in ten, so you're wrong to use it for heavy losses.

entries.name: Exaggeration
entries.definition: Overstating a key step in an argument so that the conclusion looks better supported than it is.
entries.example: Everyone knows the new rule has been a total disaster, so it must be repealed.

entries.name: Exclusive premises
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from a syllogism whose premises are both negative. Two denials do not connect the terms.
entries.example: No fish are mammals. No birds are fish. So no birds are mammals (or: so all birds are mammals).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Fallacy of exclusive premises"

entries.name: Existential fallacy
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion that says something exists from premises that are only universal ('all' or 'no') and so don't guarantee that anything exists.
entries.example: All trespassers will be fined. So some trespassers will be fined.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Fine if it is separately known that the class has members.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Quantification fallacies", item "Existential fallacy"

entries.name: Fake precision
entries.definition: Presenting a figure as more exact than the evidence can support, which gives it unearned authority.
entries.example: This policy will save exactly 1,483,227 jobs.

entries.name: Fallacy of exhaustive effort
entries.definition: Assuming that when some conditions for the best outcome can't be met, meeting as many of the rest as possible must give the next-best outcome.
entries.example: We can't have the ideal team of five, so hiring four of the five ideal people must be the next-best option (although the fifth role was what tied them together).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Fallacy of exhaustive effort"

entries.name: Fallacy of the sheep
entries.definition: Comparing raw counts between groups of very different sizes instead of comparing rates.
entries.example: There were ten cases among right-handers and only one among left-handers, so left-handed people are safer.

entries.name: False analogy
entries.definition: Arguing that because two things are alike in some ways they are alike in another way, when the similarities are not relevant to that point or the differences matter more.
entries.example: Employees are like nails: they work best when you hit them on the head.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Analogies are reasonable when the shared features are the ones that bear on the conclusion.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Analogy"

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "False analogy"

entries.name: False attribution
entries.definition: Supporting an argument with a source that is fabricated, unidentified, irrelevant, unqualified or biased, or with words a person never said.
entries.example: As Einstein said, 'Compound interest is the most powerful force in the universe.'

entries.name: False balance
entries.definition: Presenting two positions as equally supported, for example in news coverage, when the evidence strongly favours one of them.
entries.example: Giving equal airtime to one climate scientist and one sceptic, as if expert opinion were evenly split.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Balance"

entries.name: False cause
entries.definition: Concluding that one thing causes another without adequate evidence for the causal link.
entries.example: Countries with more Nobel laureates eat more chocolate, so chocolate makes people smarter.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Cause"

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Non Causa Pro Causa"

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: False dilemma
entries.definition: Presenting too few options, often just two, as the only ones, when others exist.
entries.example: Either we cut the school's art programme or we go bankrupt.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Fine when the options really are exhaustive.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Dilemma"

entries.name: False equivalence
entries.definition: Treating two things as equal or comparable because they share some feature, when they differ in ways that matter.
entries.example: Both of them told lies, so the man who misstated his age is as dishonest as the man who committed fraud.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Equivalence"

entries.name: Far-fetched hypothesis
entries.definition: Offering a bizarre explanation as the correct one without first ruling out simpler, more likely explanations.
entries.example: The crop circles must have been made by aliens.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Far-Fetched Hypothesis"

entries.name: Faulty comparison
entries.definition: Making a point by comparing something with the wrong thing, or in the wrong way.
entries.example: Our diet soda has fewer calories than a cheeseburger.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Faulty Comparison"

entries.name: Feedback fallacy
entries.definition: Trusting an evaluation as objective, and acting on it, without checking whether its source is disinterested.
entries.example: My manager says I'm the problem, so I must be (the manager is defending his own decisions).

entries.name: Form of expression (Aristotle)
entries.definition: Being misled by the grammatical form of a word into treating it as belonging to the wrong category, for example treating a word that sounds like an action as if it named an action.
entries.example: 'Flourishing' ends in -ing like 'running', so flourishing must be something a person does.

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: Formal fallacy
entries.definition: Any argument whose form is invalid: the conclusion does not follow from the premises by structure alone, so true premises could still yield a false conclusion.
entries.example: Some doctors are runners. Some runners are teenagers. So some doctors are teenagers.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Invalid Reasoning"

entries.name: Four terms
entries.definition: A syllogism that uses four distinct terms instead of three, often because one word is used in two senses, so the premises never actually connect.
entries.example: Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A sandwich is better than nothing. So a sandwich is better than eternal happiness.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Four Terms"

sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Fallacy of four terms"

entries.name: Furtive fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that outcomes must have been caused by the hidden wrongdoing of people in charge.
entries.example: The project failed, so someone must have sabotaged it.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Furtive fallacy"

entries.name: Gambler's fallacy
entries.definition: Believing that past outcomes of a random, independent process change the odds of the next outcome, so that a result is 'due'.
entries.example: Red has come up six times in a row, so black is due.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Not fallacious when outcomes really are dependent, as when cards are drawn without replacement.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Gambler's fallacy"

entries.name: Garden of forking paths
entries.definition: Assuming a single study can't suffer from the multiple-comparisons problem, when many choices about how to analyse the data were made after seeing it.
entries.example: We only ran one test, so the result can't be a fluke (after choosing which subgroup and which outcome to test once the data were in).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Garden of forking paths fallacy"

entries.name: Genetic fallacy
entries.definition: Judging a claim or practice good or bad by where it came from rather than by its present merits.
entries.example: The idea for that law was first floated in a bar, so it can't be serious.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Origins matter when the question is about reliability of a source, such as whether a document is authentic.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Genetic fallacy"

entries.name: Goomba fallacy
entries.definition: Pinning views expressed by different people in a crowd onto the crowd as a whole, then calling the group inconsistent.
entries.example: Critics say the film is too long and also say it's too rushed. Make up your minds!

entries.name: Group think
entries.definition: Substituting loyalty to or pride in one's group for reasons, so that the group's view is accepted without examination.
entries.example: Our team has decided, and questioning it would be disloyal.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Group Think"

entries.name: Guilt by association
entries.definition: Judging a claim or person by the company they keep or the groups they're linked to, rather than on the merits.
entries.example: A dictator once supported this policy, so it must be bad.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Guilt by Association"

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Association fallacy"

entries.name: Hasty generalization
entries.definition: Drawing a general conclusion from too few cases to support it.
entries.example: My two neighbours from that city were rude, so people from that city are rude.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hasty Generalization"

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Small Sample"

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Insufficient Statistics"

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Hasty generalization"

entries.name: Hedging
entries.definition: Quietly qualifying a claim to dodge counterevidence and then acting as if the original, stronger claim still stood.
entries.example: I said the stock would rise, and I meant eventually, in some sense.

entries.name: Historian's fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that people in the past had the information we have now, and judging their decisions accordingly.
entries.example: The generals should have known the attack was coming; it's obvious from the records we have now.

entries.name: Historical fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that a result came about only because a particular process was performed, when the process may have nothing to do with it.
entries.example: Our children turned out well because we followed this parenting book.

entries.name: Homunculus fallacy
entries.definition: Explaining something by appeal to a smaller version of the same thing, which leaves the original question unanswered.
entries.example: We see because a little viewer in the brain looks at the images from our eyes.

entries.name: Hot hand fallacy
entries.definition: Believing that a streak of successes in a chance process makes further successes more likely.
entries.example: I've won five hands in a row, so I'm on a hot streak and should bet more.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Where skill or condition really varies, a streak can be real evidence; the error is assuming it for pure chance.

entries.name: Hyperbolic discounting
entries.definition: Giving a small immediate reward far too much weight against a larger later reward, in a way that is inconsistent over time.
entries.example: I'd rather have $50 now than $100 in a month, though I'd choose $100 in 13 months over $50 in 12.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hyperbolic Discounting"

entries.name: Ideology-driven argumentation
entries.definition: Presupposing parts of one's own ideology that one can't defend, and treating them as settled in an argument.
entries.example: Since the free market always produces the best outcome, any regulation is harmful.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Ideology-Driven Argumentation"

entries.name: If-by-whiskey
entries.definition: Answering a question by supporting both sides, using emotionally loaded terms so that each side hears agreement.
entries.example: If by 'growth' you mean jobs for families, I'm for it; if you mean concrete over our parks, I'm against it.

entries.name: Illicit contraposition
entries.definition: Applying contraposition (swap and negate both terms) to a categorical statement where it is not valid, such as 'No A are B' or 'Some A are B'.
entries.example: No cats are dogs. So no non-dogs are non-cats.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Contraposition is valid for 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not B'.

entries.name: Illicit conversion
entries.definition: Swapping the subject and predicate of a categorical statement where the swap is not valid, such as going from 'All A are B' to 'All B are A'.
entries.example: All surgeons are doctors, so all doctors are surgeons.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Conversion is valid for 'No A are B' and 'Some A are B'.

entries.name: Illicit major
aliases: illicit process of the major term
entries.definition: A syllogism whose conclusion says something about all of the major term's class when the major premise said something about only part of it.
entries.example: All dogs are mammals. No cats are dogs. So no cats are mammals.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Illicit major"

entries.name: Illicit minor
aliases: illicit process of the minor term
entries.definition: A syllogism whose conclusion says something about all of the minor term's class when the minor premise said something about only part of it.
entries.example: All squares are rectangles. All squares are shapes. So all shapes are rectangles.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Illicit minor"

entries.name: Illicit process
entries.definition: The general name for illicit major and illicit minor: a term covers its whole class in the conclusion but not in the premise where it appears.
entries.example: All bankers are rich. No teachers are bankers. So no teachers are rich.

entries.name: Improper transposition
entries.definition: Inferring 'If not P then not Q' from 'If P then Q'. The valid move is 'If not Q then not P'.
entries.example: If you study, you'll pass. So if you don't study, you won't pass.

entries.name: Inconsistency
entries.definition: Holding or arguing from a set of claims that cannot all be true together.
entries.example: I never generalize, because people who generalize are always hypocrites.

entries.name: Independence fallacy
entries.definition: Treating events as independent and multiplying their probabilities when they are in fact linked, which can make a combination look far rarer than it is.
entries.example: Each of the plane's two engines fails once in 10,000 flights, so both failing on one flight is a 1-in-100-million event (ignoring that they share fuel and maintenance).

entries.name: Inductive conversion
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'all (or most) A are B' to 'all (or most) B are A'.
entries.example: Most jockeys are short, so most short people are jockeys.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Inductive Conversion"

entries.name: Inflation of conflict
entries.definition: Arguing that because experts disagree on some point, nothing can be known in that field or the field as a whole is unreliable.
entries.example: Economists argue about interest rates, so economics is just guesswork.

entries.name: Intensional fallacy
entries.definition: Treating different descriptions of the same object as interchangeable in contexts where the description matters, such as reports of what someone said, believed or meant, or claims about what is necessary.
entries.example: Lena believes the author of that anonymous novel is brilliant. Unknown to her, the author is her dentist. So Lena believes her dentist is brilliant.

entries.name: Intentional fallacy
entries.definition: Insisting that a text or statement can only mean what its author intended, regardless of how it actually reads.
entries.example: The author says it's not about war, so the war allegory everyone sees isn't there.

entries.name: Inverse gambler's fallacy
entries.definition: Concluding from one unlikely outcome that the process behind it must have been repeated many times before.
entries.example: He rolled double sixes on his first throw, so he must have been playing for hours.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Inverse gambler's fallacy"

entries.name: Ipse dixit
entries.definition: Presenting a claim as true without support, as if it were self-evident or as if the speaker's say-so settled it.
entries.example: It's simply true that this is the best policy. End of story.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Ipse dixit"

entries.name: Irrelevant conclusion
entries.definition: Offering an argument that may be fine in itself but supports a different conclusion from the one at issue.
entries.example: The defendant can't be guilty of fraud; the fraud caused great suffering and fraud is a terrible crime (which argues that fraud is bad, not that he did it).

entries.name: Is-ought fallacy
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion about what ought to be from premises that only say what is, without a premise that bridges the two.
entries.example: People have always eaten meat, so people ought to eat meat.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Valid if a value premise is supplied, such as 'we ought to do what keeps people healthy'.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Is–ought fallacy"

entries.name: Jumping to conclusions
entries.definition: Reaching a conclusion too quickly, without looking at relevant evidence that could easily have been checked.
entries.example: The lights are off at her house, so she must have moved away.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Quick conclusions are reasonable when the stakes are low or there's no time to gather more evidence.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hasty Conclusion"

entries.name: Kettle logic
entries.definition: Offering several defences that contradict each other, in the hope that one will work.
entries.example: I never borrowed your kettle; it was already broken; and anyway I gave it back undamaged.

entries.name: Lack of proportion
entries.definition: Exaggerating, downplaying or failing to notice the real importance of a point, so it gets the wrong weight in the reasoning.
entries.example: One typo in the report means none of its findings can be trusted.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Lack of Proportion"

entries.name: Line-drawing fallacy
entries.definition: Concluding that because no sharp line can be drawn between two things, there is no real difference between them, or that a vague term can't be used.
entries.example: One more grain doesn't make a heap, so there's no such thing as a heap of sand.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Bald Man"

entries.name: Loaded label
entries.definition: Using a descriptive label whose connotations assume the point in dispute.
entries.example: This 'death tax' should be repealed.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: An evocative label is not itself fallacious when the argument doesn't depend on it.

sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Improper premise", item "Loaded label"

entries.name: Loaded language
entries.definition: Using emotionally charged or value-laden words, in what is presented as a neutral argument, to push the listener toward a conclusion.
entries.example: The bureaucrats' job-killing scheme will be voted on today.

entries.name: Logic chopping
entries.definition: Obscuring the issue with needlessly technical distinctions or formal machinery that don't bear on the real question.
entries.example: Before we discuss the budget, define 'spending' in predicate logic.

entries.name: Lottery fallacy
entries.definition: Treating an outcome as too improbable to be chance because that particular outcome was unlikely, while ignoring that some unlikely outcome was bound to happen.
entries.example: The odds that she in particular would win were 1 in 10 million, so the draw must have been rigged.

entries.name: Ludic fallacy
entries.definition: Treating real-world uncertainty as if it followed the neat, known odds of a game or model, overlooking unknown risks.
entries.example: Our model treats market moves like coin flips, so a crash this size is effectively impossible.

entries.name: Lump of labour fallacy
entries.definition: Treating the total amount of work in an economy as fixed, so that every job taken by one person or machine must be a job lost by another.
entries.example: If older people work longer, there will be fewer jobs for the young.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies", item "Lump of labour fallacy"

entries.name: Lying
entries.definition: An argument that depends on a statement the speaker knows to be false.
entries.example: As everyone at the meeting agreed (they didn't), we should approve the merger.

entries.name: Magical thinking
entries.definition: Assuming a causal link between events that have no plausible connection, such as between thoughts, rituals or symbols and outside events.
entries.example: If I think about the accident, it might happen.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Magical thinking"

entries.name: Masked man fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that if two names or descriptions pick out the same thing, they can be swapped inside statements about what someone knows, believes or wants.
entries.example: I know who my father is. I don't know who the masked man is. So the masked man is not my father.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hooded Man"

entries.name: McNamara fallacy
entries.definition: Deciding only on what can easily be measured and treating what can't be measured as unimportant or nonexistent.
entries.example: Test scores went up, so the school is better, never mind whether students learn to think.

entries.name: Middle ground
entries.definition: Taking it for granted that the truth must lie halfway between two opposing positions.
entries.example: You say the bridge needs 10 tonnes of steel; he says 2. Let's use 6.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Compromise can be wise in negotiation; the error is treating it as a test of truth.

entries.name: Mind projection fallacy
entries.definition: Treating a feature of how we perceive or know something as if it were a property of the thing itself.
entries.example: The coin toss is random, so randomness is a physical property of the coin.

entries.name: Misleading vividness
entries.definition: Letting a few dramatic, memorable cases outweigh a larger body of statistical evidence.
entries.example: I saw a terrible shark attack on the news, so swimming at the beach is too dangerous.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misleading Vividness"

entries.name: Misplaced burden of proof
entries.definition: Demanding that others prove you wrong when it is your job to support your own claim.
entries.example: I say this herb cures colds. Prove it doesn't.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misplaced Burden of Proof"

entries.name: Modal scope fallacy
entries.definition: Treating 'necessarily, if P then Q' as if it were 'if P, then necessarily Q', so that a merely true conclusion is wrongly presented as a necessary one.
entries.example: Necessarily, if you are married you have a spouse. You are married. So you necessarily have a spouse (as if you could not have stayed single).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Modal scope fallacy"

entries.name: Moralistic fallacy
entries.definition: Inferring what is the case from what ought to be the case, for example concluding that something can't be true because it would be bad if it were.
entries.example: People shouldn't be unequal in ability, so there are no differences in ability.

entries.name: Motte-and-bailey
entries.definition: Defending a bold, controversial claim by retreating to a modest, easy-to-defend claim when challenged, then returning to the bold claim once the challenge passes.
entries.example: 'Medicine is a scam.' Challenged: 'I just mean drug companies sometimes put profit first.'

entries.name: Moving the goalposts
entries.definition: Demanding new or greater evidence once the evidence originally asked for has been supplied.
entries.example: You showed me one study? Show me ten. Ten? They must be from other countries.

entries.name: Multiple comparisons fallacy
entries.definition: Making many comparisons in one set of data and then treating a 'significant' result as meaningful, without allowing for the fact that some will turn up by chance.
entries.example: We checked 40 foods against 40 diseases and found that eating celery is linked to ear infections.

entries.name: Naturalistic fallacy
entries.definition: Defining or inferring what is good from some natural property, such as what is pleasant or what evolved; in the broad sense, any move from facts alone to values.
entries.example: Pleasure is what people desire, so pleasure is what is good.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Naturalistic fallacy"

entries.name: Naturalistic fallacy fallacy
entries.definition: Rejecting any argument from facts to values as a naturalistic fallacy even when it supplies the value premises needed to make it work.
entries.example: You can't argue that smoking is bad because it causes cancer. That's deriving an ought from an is!

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Naturalistic fallacy fallacy"

entries.name: Negative conclusion from affirmative premises
entries.definition: A syllogism with only affirmative premises but a negative conclusion.
entries.example: All pets are tame. Some birds are pets. So some birds are not tame.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Negative conclusion from affirmative premises"

entries.name: Nirvana fallacy
entries.definition: Rejecting a solution because it isn't perfect, rather than comparing it with realistic alternatives.
entries.example: Seatbelts don't prevent all deaths, so there's no point wearing them.

entries.name: No true Scotsman
entries.definition: Protecting a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group so that the counterexample doesn't count.
entries.example: No true environmentalist flies. She flies? Then she's not a true environmentalist.

entries.name: Non sequitur
entries.definition: A conclusion that doesn't follow from the reasons given, because they are irrelevant to it or far too weak.
entries.example: She's an excellent cook, so she'll make a fine senator.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Non Sequitur"

entries.name: Nut-picking
entries.definition: Finding the most extreme or fringe members of an opposing group and presenting them as typical of the whole group.
entries.example: Look at this one ranting post; that's what all supporters of that policy are like.

entries.name: Obscurum per obscurius
aliases: explaining the obscure by the more obscure
entries.definition: Explaining something unclear by appeal to something even less clear.
entries.example: Consciousness is just the quantum vibration of universal mind.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Obscurum per Obscurius"

entries.name: Observational interpretation fallacy
entries.definition: Reading an association found in an observational study as proof of cause and effect.
entries.example: People who drink coffee in this survey live longer, so coffee extends life.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: An association can be a reason to test for causation, for example with a controlled experiment.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Observational interpretation fallacy"

entries.name: Opposition
entries.definition: Opposing an argument simply because of the person or camp it comes from, such as a rival party, without engaging its content.
entries.example: That's a proposal from the other party, so we're against it.

entries.name: Over-extrapolation
entries.definition: Extending a trend far beyond the range of data that support it, as if it would continue indefinitely.
entries.example: The child grew 8 cm this year, so by age 40 he'll be over 4 metres tall.

entries.name: Overgenerality
entries.definition: Using a concept or claim so broad that it gives no useful information in context, often to avoid committing to anything checkable.
entries.example: My plan for the economy is to make things better for people.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Broad terms are fine when the context doesn't call for anything more specific.

entries.name: Oversimplification
entries.definition: Covering up relevant complexity and making a problem look simpler than it is, so that a conclusion seems better supported.
entries.example: Crime is down because we hired more police. That's all there is to it.

entries.name: Overwhelming exception
entries.definition: A generalization stated with so many qualifications that what is left is much weaker than the headline claim suggests.
entries.example: All our customers are satisfied, apart from those who complained, returned the product, or didn't respond.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"

entries.name: P-hacking
entries.definition: Trying many analyses or experiments and reporting only the ones that cross the significance threshold, so the reported result looks stronger than it is.
entries.example: We ran twenty versions of the study and published the one that reached p < 0.05.

entries.name: Package deal
entries.definition: Treating things that are essentially different as if they formed one unit because they are often grouped together.
entries.example: If you support free speech, you must support every view people express with it.

entries.name: Pathetic fallacy
entries.definition: Holding a mistaken belief because you attribute human feelings or purposes to inanimate things.
entries.example: The storm is angry at us for building on this coast.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: As a deliberate figure of speech in literature it is not an error of reasoning.

entries.name: Persuasive definition
entries.definition: Winning an argument by getting others to accept a slanted definition of a key term that builds in the desired conclusion.
entries.example: Real art means beautiful art, so this abstract painting isn't real art.

entries.name: Poisoning the well
entries.definition: Discrediting a person in advance, before they speak, so that anything they say will be dismissed.
entries.example: Before you hear from my opponent, remember that he's a paid lobbyist who'll say anything.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

entries.name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: after this, therefore because of this
entries.definition: Concluding that because B happened after A, A caused B.
entries.example: I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks helped us win.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Order in time is one piece of evidence for causation, but needs support from other evidence.

entries.name: Proof by assertion
entries.definition: Restating a claim again and again, regardless of objections, as if repeating it proved it.
entries.example: This diet works. It works. I've told you a hundred times: it works.

entries.name: Proof surrogate
entries.definition: Substituting a phrase that suggests proof, such as 'everyone knows' or 'studies show', for actual evidence.
entries.example: Any reasonable person can see the plan is sound, and experts agree.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

entries.name: Prosecutor's fallacy
entries.definition: Confusing the chance of the evidence given innocence with the chance of innocence given the evidence, which overstates how strongly evidence points to guilt.
entries.example: Only 1 in a million people would match this blood type, so there is only a 1 in a million chance the defendant is innocent.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Prosecutor's Fallacy"

entries.name: Proving too much
entries.definition: An argument that, if it worked, would also establish conclusions that are clearly false, showing that something in it is wrong.
entries.example: You can't ban guns because some people use them responsibly (which would also rule out banning anything).

entries.name: Psychologist's fallacy
entries.definition: An observer assumes their own perspective is objective and reads it into the behaviour or experience they are studying.
entries.example: I would have felt humiliated in that situation, so the subject must have felt humiliated.

entries.name: Quantifier shift
entries.definition: Swapping the order of 'every' and 'some': moving from 'everything has some X' to 'there is one X that everything has'.
entries.example: Every child has a mother. So there is one woman who is the mother of every child.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Every and All"

entries.name: Question-begging analogy
entries.definition: An argument by analogy whose force depends on the very point in dispute.
entries.example: Eating meat is like eating people, so it's wrong.

entries.name: Questionable premise
entries.definition: Relying on a premise that the audience has good reason to doubt, without supporting it.
entries.example: Since all politicians are corrupt, we shouldn't trust this one.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Questionable Premise"

entries.name: Quibbling
entries.definition: Complaining about a minor point as if that undermined the whole argument.
entries.example: You wrote 'less' instead of 'fewer', so your argument about the budget is worthless.

entries.name: Quoting out of context
entries.definition: Quoting someone selectively so that the context that fixes their meaning is lost and they appear to say something else.
entries.example: The critic called the film 'a triumph ... of marketing over substance', and the poster says 'a triumph!'.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies", item "Fallacy of quoting out of context"

entries.name: Rationalization
entries.definition: Offering reasons that are not the real reasons for a belief or action, chosen to make it look more acceptable.
entries.example: I bought the sports car for its safety rating.

entries.name: Red herring
entries.definition: Bringing in an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the issue under discussion.
entries.example: Why worry about the factory's pollution when so many people need jobs?

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Red Herring"

entries.name: Redefinition
entries.definition: Giving a familiar term a new meaning and then slipping between the new and the ordinary meanings in the course of an argument.
entries.example: Counting everyone under 25 as 'youth', youth unemployment is high, so teenagers can't find summer jobs.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Giving a term a new technical meaning is fine if it is used consistently.

entries.name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
entries.definition: A form of guilt by association: discrediting a view because Hitler or the Nazis held it or something like it.
entries.example: Hitler was a vegetarian, so vegetarianism is suspect.

entries.name: Referential fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that every word refers to a real thing and that a word's meaning is just the thing it refers to.
entries.example: We have a word for 'luck', so luck must be a force in the world.

entries.name: Regression fallacy
entries.definition: Crediting a cause for a change that is just extreme results drifting back toward the average.
entries.example: After her worst game of the season she wore a new bracelet, and next game she played better. The bracelet works.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Regression fallacy"

entries.name: Reification
entries.definition: Treating an abstraction, such as 'society', 'nature' or 'the market', as if it were a concrete thing or agent with its own will.
entries.example: The market wants lower interest rates, so the central bank should obey it.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Speaking figuratively is fine as long as the argument doesn't depend on the abstraction actually acting.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misplaced Concreteness"

entries.name: Relative privation
entries.definition: Dismissing a problem or complaint because worse problems exist elsewhere.
entries.example: Why complain about potholes when people in other countries have no roads?
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Comparisons are relevant when the actual question is how to rank priorities.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Fallacy of relative privation"

entries.name: Retrospective determinism
entries.definition: Assuming that because something happened under certain circumstances, those circumstances made it inevitable.
entries.example: The company collapsed, so its collapse was bound to happen from the day it was founded.

entries.name: Reversing causation
entries.definition: Getting cause and effect the wrong way round.
entries.example: Hospitals are full of sick people, so hospitals make people sick.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Reversing Causation"

sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Wrong direction"

entries.name: Scapegoating
entries.definition: Unfairly blaming an unpopular person or group for a problem.
entries.example: The product launch failed because of the new intern.

entries.name: Scope fallacy
entries.definition: Misreading or shifting how much of a sentence a word like 'not', 'all' or 'necessarily' applies to, and drawing a conclusion from the wrong reading.
entries.example: 'Everyone isn't coming' means no one is coming, so the party is cancelled (when the speaker meant 'not everyone is coming').

entries.name: Secundum quid
aliases: a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter
entries.definition: Aristotle's fallacy of treating something true only in a certain respect, or with a qualification, as if it were true without qualification.
entries.example: He's a good thief, and someone who is good is a good person, so he is a good person.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Secundum Quid"

entries.name: Selective attention
entries.definition: Focusing on some aspects of a situation while ignoring others that are relevant.
entries.example: 'How was school?' 'I got an A in art!' (the four failed tests go unmentioned).

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Selective Attention"

entries.name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
entries.definition: Treating the fulfilment of a prediction as confirming it, when the act of predicting helped bring the outcome about.
entries.example: I told everyone the bank would fail; the run on the bank proved me right.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy"

entries.name: Self-selection
entries.definition: A biased generalization where the sample consists of people who chose to take part, and so tend to differ from those who didn't.
entries.example: Readers who wrote in overwhelmingly favour the new policy, so the public favours it.

entries.name: Fallacy of the single cause
entries.definition: Assuming an outcome has one simple cause when it actually arose from several causes acting together.
entries.example: The war started because an archduke was shot.

entries.name: Slanting
entries.definition: Presenting an issue unfairly by selective emphasis, suppression or misdescription of the evidence.
entries.example: The report described the protest's one broken window in detail and never mentioned the thousands who marched peacefully.

entries.name: Slippery slope
entries.definition: Claiming that a first step will lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without good reason to think each step will actually follow.
entries.example: If we let students redo one test, soon they'll expect to redo every test, and degrees will be worthless.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Fine when there is real evidence that each step is likely to follow the one before it.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Slippery Slope"

entries.name: Smear tactic
entries.definition: An unfair, damaging characterization of an opponent or their position, meant to discredit rather than to answer.
entries.example: My opponent, who never met a tax he didn't love, wants to 'reform' the budget.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Smear Tactic"

entries.name: Smokescreen
entries.definition: Offering so many details or side issues that the main point, or the evidence against it, is obscured.
entries.example: Responding to one question about safety with a 40-page technical appendix nobody can parse.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Clouding the Issue"

entries.name: Some are / some are not
entries.definition: Inferring 'Some A are not B' from 'Some A are B', or the reverse. 'Some' does not logically mean 'not all'.
entries.example: Some of the samples are contaminated, so some of them are clean.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: In conversation 'some' often hints 'not all', but that hint is not a logical consequence.

entries.name: Special pleading
entries.definition: Applying a rule or standard to others while exempting yourself or a favoured case without justifying the exception.
entries.example: Everyone should obey the speed limit, but I'm a good driver, so I can go faster.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Exceptions are fine when a relevant difference is actually shown.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Special Pleading"

entries.name: Specificity
entries.definition: Drawing a more specific conclusion than the evidence supports.
entries.example: The trails were dug by an animal, so a badger dug them last Tuesday night.

entries.name: Stereotyping
entries.definition: Treating a stereotype as if it were an accurate generalization about every member of a group.
entries.example: She's an accountant, so she must be boring.

entries.name: Straw man
entries.definition: Misrepresenting someone's position as a weaker or more extreme version and then attacking that version instead of what they actually hold.
entries.example: She wants stricter emissions rules. So she wants to ban cars and make us all ride bicycles.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Straw Man"

entries.name: Style over substance
entries.definition: Treating the polish, confidence or catchiness of how an argument is delivered as if it added to how strong the argument is.
entries.example: Vote for Ray, he will save the day! (a slogan offered in place of a reason to prefer him)

entries.name: Subjectivist fallacy
aliases: true for you, not for me
entries.definition: Rejecting a claim on the grounds that truth is just a matter of opinion, when the claim is about objective fact.
entries.example: Maybe the earth is round for you, but that's not my truth.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Some claims, such as about personal taste, really are subjective.

entries.name: Sunk cost fallacy
entries.definition: Continuing with something because of what has already been spent on it, rather than judging it on its future costs and benefits.
entries.example: We've already spent two years on this failing project, so we have to keep going.

entries.name: Superstitious thinking
entries.definition: Reasoning from grounds that are well known to be unreliable, such as omens or lucky charms.
entries.example: A black cat crossed my path, so I'll cancel the interview.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Superstitious Thinking"

entries.name: Suppressed correlative
entries.definition: Redefining one of a pair of contrasting terms so that the other has nothing left to apply to.
entries.example: I'm not fat; John is fatter than me, so only John counts as fat.

entries.name: Suppressed evidence
entries.definition: Leaving out relevant evidence that tells against your conclusion, or selecting only the evidence that supports it.
entries.example: Our drug helped 30 patients (we won't mention the 70 it didn't).

entries.name: Survivorship bias
entries.definition: Drawing conclusions from the cases that made it through some filter while ignoring the ones that didn't.
entries.example: All the famous dropouts became billionaires, so dropping out is a good career move.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Survivorship bias"

entries.name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
entries.definition: Picking out a cluster or pattern after looking at the data, then treating it as meaningful as if it had been predicted beforehand (like painting a target around bullet holes).
entries.example: Five people on this street got sick, so something on this street is causing it (out of thousands of streets, some will have clusters by chance).

entries.name: Thought-terminating cliché
entries.definition: Using a stock phrase to end discussion rather than to answer the point.
entries.example: It is what it is.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Thought-terminating cliché"

entries.name: Tokenism
entries.definition: Accepting a token gesture as if it were an adequate substitute for real action.
entries.example: The company planted ten trees, so it clearly cares about the environment.

entries.name: Tone policing
entries.definition: Dismissing an argument because of the emotion or manner in which it is delivered rather than its content.
entries.example: I'll listen to your complaint once you calm down.

entries.name: Traitorous critic fallacy
aliases: if you don't like it, leave
entries.definition: Answering criticism by attacking the critic's loyalty and telling them to leave, instead of addressing the criticism.
entries.example: If you hate this country's healthcare so much, move somewhere else.

entries.name: Tu quoque
entries.definition: Dismissing a claim or criticism because the person making it doesn't live up to it themselves.
entries.example: You say smoking is bad for me, but you smoke.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Pointing out hypocrisy is fair when the question is the person's consistency or sincerity rather than the truth of what they say.

entries.name: Two wrongs make a right
entries.definition: Defending a wrong action because someone else did something wrong, as if one wrong cancels another.
entries.example: He cheated on the last test, so it's fine for me to cheat on this one.

entries.name: Undistributed middle
entries.definition: A categorical syllogism in which the middle term (the one shared by both premises) never covers all members of its class, so the premises fail to link the other two terms.
entries.example: All spies wear sunglasses. My neighbor wears sunglasses. So my neighbor is a spy.

entries.name: Unfalsifiability
entries.definition: Offering an explanation that no possible evidence could count against, and treating that as a strength.
entries.example: The cure works for those with enough faith; if it didn't work for you, your faith was too weak.

entries.name: Unrepresentative sample
entries.definition: Generalizing about a population from a sample that was gathered in a way likely to differ from that population.
entries.example: Our website poll shows 80% of people love our product.

entries.name: Vacuous truth (misuse)
entries.definition: Offering a claim that is technically true only because there is nothing for it to be about, as if it were informative.
entries.example: None of our cars have ever failed a safety test (we've never had one tested).

entries.name: Vagueness (exploiting)
entries.definition: Relying on a word with fuzzy boundaries so that a claim can't be tested or pinned down, or so that it seems to cover more than it does.
entries.example: This supplement supports wellness.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Vague words are often unavoidable and fine; the problem is when the argument depends on the vagueness.

entries.name: Vested interest
entries.definition: Arguing that a claim is wrong, or a proposal should be rejected, only because the person advancing it would benefit.
entries.example: The union backs the safety rule because it helps union members, so the rule is a bad idea.

entries.name: Willed ignorance
entries.definition: Refusing to consider evidence or arguments against a view one has already decided to hold.
entries.example: I've decided the treatment works, and I'm not reading any more studies about it.

entries.name: Wishful thinking
entries.definition: Believing or rejecting a claim because of how much you want it to be so, rather than because of evidence.
entries.example: The tumour must be benign. I can't bear to think otherwise.
entries.not_a_fallacy_when: Hope can be a reasonable motive for action; it isn't evidence.
